title: Snapshot Array
description:
# Snapshot Array

Implement a `SnapshotArray` that behaves like an integer array with persistent snapshots. All elements are initially `0`.

Implement the `SnapshotArray` class:

*   `SnapshotArray(int length)` initializes an array-like data structure with the given `length`.
*   `void set(int index, int val)` sets the element at `index` to `val` for the current working version.
*   `int snap()` stores the current working version and returns its `snap_id`. The first call returns `0`, the second returns `1`, and so on.
*   `int get(int index, int snap_id)` returns the value at `index` in the snapshot identified by `snap_id`.

A value written after a snapshot must not change that older snapshot. Repeated `set` calls to the same index before the same `snap()` only need the final value for that snapshot.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:**
["SnapshotArray","set","snap","set","get"]
[[3],[0,5],[],[0,6],[0,0]]
**Output:**
[null,null,0,null,5]
**Explanation:**
SnapshotArray snapshotArr = new SnapshotArray(3); // length is 3
snapshotArr.set(0,5);  // working array[0] = 5
snapshotArr.snap();    // stores snapshot 0
snapshotArr.set(0,6);  // changes only the working version
snapshotArr.get(0,0);  // returns 5 from snapshot 0

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= length <= 5 * 10^4`
*   `0 <= index < length`
*   `0 <= val <= 10^9`
*   `0 <= snap_id <` the number of times `snap()` has been called
*   At most `5 * 10^4` calls will be made to `set`, `snap`, and `get`.

solutions.name: TreeMap per Index with Floor Entry
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log S) per set and get, O(1) per snap
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep one `TreeMap<Integer, Integer>` for each array index. The map stores only values written at particular snapshot ids, seeded with `(0, 0)` for the default value. `set` writes the current `snapId`, `snap` returns and increments it, and `get` asks the map for the latest entry whose key is not greater than the requested `snap_id`.

## Key Insight

A snapshot value is the last assignment at or before that snapshot id. `floorEntry` is exactly that predecessor query, so old snapshots stay stable when later writes use larger ids.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log S) for `set` and `get`, O(1) for `snap`, where S is the number of writes at one index.
- Space Complexity: O(n + S) over all stored changes.

solutions.name: ArrayList Change Log with Binary Search
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) amortized per set, O(1) per snap, O(log S) per get
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each index, keep an ordered list of `(snap_id, value)` pairs. The first pair is `(0, 0)`. A `set` in the same working snapshot updates the last pair instead of appending another one; otherwise it appends a new pair. `get` binary-searches for the last pair whose `snap_id` is at most the requested id.

## Key Insight

Repeated writes before the same `snap()` collapse to the final value, but the list remains sorted by `snap_id`. That gives compact storage and logarithmic historical lookup.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) amortized for `set`, O(1) for `snap`, and O(log S) for `get`.
- Space Complexity: O(n + S).

solutions.name: Sparse HashMap Histories
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) amortized per set, O(1) per snap, O(log S) per get
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store histories only for indexes that have ever been written. A hash map maps an index to its ordered list of `(snap_id, value)` pairs. Untouched indexes return `0` immediately. Written indexes use the same same-snapshot overwrite rule and binary search as the dense per-index list.

## Key Insight

The array can be large while the number of writes is limited. Allocating history lists lazily keeps untouched indexes at zero without building `length` lists up front.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) amortized for `set`, O(1) for `snap`, and O(log S) for `get` on a touched index.
- Space Complexity: O(S), where S is the number of stored changes.

solutions.name: Pending Writes Committed at Snap
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) per set, O(k) per snap, O(log S) per get
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep a pending map for writes made since the previous snapshot. `set` only updates this pending map, so repeated writes to the same index before `snap()` are naturally coalesced. During `snap`, commit each pending index's final value into that index history under the snapshot id being returned.

## Key Insight

The committed history represents completed snapshots, while pending writes represent the current working version. This separation makes it explicit that `get` can only read already-taken snapshots.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) for `set`, O(k) for `snap` over k changed indexes, and O(log S) for `get`.
- Space Complexity: O(n + S).

solutions.name: Primitive Dynamic Arrays per Index
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) amortized per set, O(1) per snap, O(log S) per get
solutions.description:
## Approach

Replace object lists with two dynamic primitive arrays per index: one array for snapshot ids and one for values. `set` overwrites the last cell when it belongs to the current snapshot, otherwise it appends and grows that index's arrays if needed. `get` binary-searches the primitive snapshot-id array.

## Key Insight

The logical structure is the same sorted change log, but storing primitive arrays reduces object overhead and makes the binary-search state visible.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) amortized for `set`, O(1) for `snap`, and O(log S) for `get`.
- Space Complexity: O(n + S).
